1000229.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Italian Monte Carlo. The Italian name literally means “Mount Charles”, from monte (“mount, mountain”) and the personal name Carlo (“Charles”). The former Spélugues district was officially named Monte-Carlo on 1 July 1866 in honour of Charles III, Prince of Monaco.
Parallel international adaptations include French Monte-Carlo, German Monte-Carlo, Polish Monte Carlo, Portuguese Monte Carlo, Slovak Monte Carlo and Spanish Montecarlo (“Monte Carlo”).

1001253.etyen:
A Norwegian female given name, either derived from the male given name Jan or contracted from Johanne. Both source names belong to the Johannes name family, ultimately from Latin Iōhannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Biblical Hebrew יְהוֹחָנָן (Yəhōḥānān, “Yahweh is gracious”).
Compare Danish Janne and Swedish Janne (“given name”).

1004837.etyen:
From vann (“water”) + kastanje (“chestnut”), literally “water chestnut”, referring to the plant's wetland habitat and to its edible brown corm, which resembles a chestnut in shape and colour and has a mildly nutlike taste. Despite the name, the plant is not closely related to true chestnuts.
Compare Danish vandkastanje, Swedish vattenkastanj and Icelandic vatnakastanía (“water chestnut”). Equivalent formations include German Wasserkastanie, Dutch waterkastanje, English water chestnut and Finnish vesikastanja.

1005093.etyen:
Borrowed from English Nancy (“female given name”), with the spelling adapted to Norwegian as Nansy.
The deeper origin of English Nancy is uncertain, but it was early used as a pet form of Ann. Under this analysis, the name belongs to the Anna name family, ultimately from Late Latin Anna (“female given name”), from Koine Greek Ἄννα (Ánna, “Anna”), from Biblical Hebrew חַנָּה (“Hannah; grace, favour”).
First attested in the late 19th c.
Compare Danish Nansy and Swedish Nansy (“female given name”), likewise spelling variants of Nancy.
